newsitem.title: USA: Balanced budget would cut interest rates - Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Balanced budget would cut interest rates - Clinton.

text.p: President Clinton on Thursday called on Congress to work with him to balance the federal budget by the year 2002, saying that that would be good for the economy and for America.

"Our work is not done," Clinton said in the preface to the fiscal year 1998 budget he formally presented to Congress on Thursday. "I urge Congress to help me finish the job and balance the budget by 2002.
In its budget proposal, the administration argues that a balanced budget deal with Congress would bring down both short and long-term interest rates.
"A bipartisan agreement this year would greatly foster chances of further cuts in both short and long-term rates," the administration said in its budget proposal.
The proposal apparently assumes no increase in short-term interest rates by the Federal Reserve this year, despite expectations to the contrary by many private experts.

Specifically, the budget expects the rate on three-month Treasury bills to hold steady at an average of five percent this year. If the budget is balanced, it sees that rate gradually falling to four percent by 2001 and holding there. The three-month bill rate is now around 5.13 percent.

The administration also sees a gradual decline in long-term interest rates if the budget is balanced, with the yield on 10-year Treasury notes projected to fall gradually to 5.1 percent by the year 2001. It is now about 6.46 percent.

"Deficit cutting can go hand-in-hand with economic growth - if the deficit cutting allows the Federal Reserve to maintain low interest rates and if it's credible with financial markets," the administration said.
It said it sees no sign of an impending economic downturn and defended the longer-range economic forecasts contained in its budget proposal as prudent.

The administration expects growth to slow to two percent annually in 1997 and 1998, before picking up to a 2.3 percent rate -- which it sees as the economy's long-term potential pace -- in the following years to 2002.
The forecast looks to have been compiled before news of the economy's stronger-than-expected 4.7 percent annualized surge in the fourth quarter of last year.

The administration said that several factors are holding the economy back. The labor force is growing more slowly than before and the economy is still working its way out from under the stagnant savings and low investment of the 1980's.
"The recent slow growth of the major European economies and Japan has constrained the exports of even the newly revitalized and competitive U.S. economy," it added.
The administration argued that the economy has already benefited greatly from the progress made in slashing the budget deficit during Clinton's first four years in office.
Among other things, it pointed to the steep rise of the stock market over that period. "Corporate profits, the underpinning for the value of stocks, also have soared," it added.
In making its case for a balanced budget, the administration also argued that the big rise in federal government debt during the 1980's hurt the economy.
"Persistent deficits reduce saving, raise interest rates, stifle investment and cut the growth of productivity, output and incomes," it said.

While foreign capital helped to make up for some of the shortfall in domestic savings during the last decade, that came at a price -- a higher dollar that sharply boosted the U.S. trade deficit, the administration said.
